finding.headline: About 18% of your pay goes to tax now; in retirement, about 3% of withdrawals would.
details: Of your $120,000 pay, about $21,410 goes to tax, leaving about $98,590. Federal tax is about $12,230, payroll tax about $9,180, and state tax is $0.
In retirement, the plan draws about $31,063 a year, and tax on that is about $1,953 a year. Your savings split is about 57% taxable and cash, 31% pre-tax, and 12% Roth.
The plan draws on taxable savings first, then pre-tax accounts like a 401(k), and Roth accounts last. This is a rough guide, not tax advice; a tax professional can check the details.

finding.headline: You plan to retire at 46, so Medicare at 65 is the key gap to plan for.
details: Medicare generally starts when you turn 65. Your Initial Enrollment Period lasts 7 months, from 3 months before you turn 65 to 3 months after that month. Your plan shows about 20 years until 65 and about 19 years without Medicare after you retire.
If you miss that 7-month window, you may have to wait to sign up and pay a monthly late enrollment penalty for as long as you have Part B. The penalty grows the longer you wait.
Social Security benefits rise for each month you delay past full retirement age, but the increase stops at age 70. Starting as early as 62 means a smaller benefit.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.

Until you retire you save about $31,690 a year: $23,000 into a 401(k) or IRA, $3,600 from your employer's match, $5,090 of take-home pay left after your spending, which the plan assumes you save. If that is wrong, change 'Yearly saving' in your answers.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $30,000 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 70, which pays about $37,200 a year.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 93. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
